subtitle: A practical guide to the current editing tools: small first edits, advanced workflows, actual editing and appearance examples, a glossary and an alphabetical index.
scope: Investigate unfamiliar cartridges without a game definition, review exact edits, create separate builds, playtest and verify patches. Named game workflows require their exact supported revision. Observations, candidate layouts and unknown behavior remain distinct.
basic_summary: Start the application, choose saved preferences, identify a source, make a focused edit, preserve progress and export a checked patch. These procedures build the habits used throughout the guide.
advanced_summary: Use explicit definitions for graphics, text, tables, connected-room layouts, audio and bounded automation. Follow declared ranges to exact bytes, and keep editor metadata, native observations and unknown game semantics separate.
attribution: By RetchEWretched. ROMancer code and original fixtures use the project MIT license. Instructional screenshots show third-party games, including Castlevania, Chrono Trigger, The Immortal, Wario Land 4, Final Fantasy Legend II and Deja Vu I & II; their imagery and trademarks remain those of their respective rights holders and are separate from the code license. No ROM files, game saves, emulator states, firmware dumps or authentication data are included in this guide. The prebuilt PDF and HTML work offline; PDF rebuilding optionally uses ReportLab.

chapters.title: Install, open and choose a workspace
chapters.intro: The full Windows x64 release includes Python, Pillow and credited emulator engines. The source edition uses your own Python installation. Both include this guide.
steps: Run the Windows setup executable. Choose the install location, finish setup, then open ROMancer. The application and its saved workspace are separate.
For the portable Windows ZIP, extract the entire archive and use Open ROMancer.cmd. Keep app, python, cores and the root launch files together.

For the source edition, install Python 3.13 or later and the pinned requirements, then use Launch ROMancer.cmd on Windows or the supplied run.sh launcher. Read the root README for the command-line and MCP entry points.
Open Help for tutorials and this guide. Start a workshop or import a ROM you supply. No AI account, subscription or API key is required.
chapters.result: ROMancer opens its local interface and your project list. The full Windows edition selects a matching included engine when you load a supported system.
chapters.note: Keep the complete folder when moving a portable copy. Moving the program does not by itself move the workspace or its projects.

details.title: Update and recovery
details.text: Install a new build revision rather than replacing files inside an old verified version. Rollback changes the active application version while preserving projects; an older application may not understand newer project features.

chapters.title: Set preferences and choose a theme
chapters.intro: Settings control the working environment: appearance, startup behavior, automatic analysis and audio defaults. Apply the choices you want to keep before closing the application.
steps: Open Settings. Review appearance and startup preferences. 100% is the standard interface size; it uses the more compact layout previously shown at 75%. Choose another offered size when useful.
Choose a theme: ROMancer (default), Dark for neutral graphite or Light for grey panels on a light background. Adjust Reduce interface motion and Show advanced tools in navigation to suit your work.

Review Auto deep scan on ROM load, enabled by default, and Inspect gameplay graphics automatically. Set Remember my workspace to reopen the last project, ROM, page and editing position. These preferences choose automatic work, not a new level of game-format verification.

Set Volume from 0 to 100, Start game audio muted and Loop audio previews. Choose Apply to save and continue, or OK to save and close. Cancel discards unapplied changes. Restore defaults prepares the standard choices; use Apply or OK to keep that reset.
chapters.result: Applied preferences persist across launches for this workspace. The chosen theme and size make the controls comfortable to read, and automatic scan/audio behavior follows the saved choices.
chapters.note: ROMancer and Dark use deeper menu backgrounds; Light uses darker grey panels and menu boxes with dark labels. Selected items and keyboard focus remain distinct. Themes change appearance, not ROM bytes. Manual investigation remains available when automatic analysis is disabled.

details.title: When to change automatic work
details.text: Leave Auto deep scan on ROM load enabled for normal discovery. Turn it off when you want to choose the timing of a manual scan. Automatic analysis of paused gameplay graphics depends on an actual loaded session and exposed data; it does not identify arbitrary resource ownership.

details.title: Audio and motion
details.text: Volume and start-muted preferences control playback defaults; use the current preview controls when listening. Preview looping repeats the available preview, not the game sequence. Reduced motion makes interface motion less distracting.

details.title: Apply, Cancel and defaults
details.text: Apply saves the currently selected preferences without closing Settings. Cancel does not roll back an earlier Apply. Restore defaults prepares the standard choices for review; use Apply or OK to keep them.

chapters.title: Your first complete edit: the original NES workshop
chapters.intro: Use the included original drawing program to learn the full workflow without finding offsets or supplying a commercial game.
steps: If the optional tutorial prompt appears, choose Not now for this exercise. Save existing work; choose the blank Choose a project entry if needed. On the empty Overview, click NES workshop.
Open Graphics & fonts. Keep First tile 0, Tiles across 1 and Tiles down 1; click Assemble tiles. Set Brush color index to 1.
Focus the Editing canvas. Press Right Arrow once, then Space. Expect 1 pixels differ; the Original picture stays unchanged. Undo sprite stroke reverses the experiment.
Click Review asset changes, read the plan, then Create asset build. Choose the new build in the top source/build selector.
Open Playtest, choose Load game, then Play. Pause to inspect the result. The full Windows edition supplies the engine; the source edition may require core setup.

Open Export. Choose the original revision and your asset build, then Create & independently verify patch. Download the prepared BPS. Continue with Apply a downloaded patch to check a fresh reconstruction.
chapters.result: The tested exercise changed exactly file offset 16400 (0x4010), from 81 to C1. Native original/build frames differed, a save/load roundtrip restored the view, and reapplying the exported patch recreated the same build hash.
chapters.note: Those byte values belong only to this original workshop. Its drawing program reuses the tile, so one edited pixel can repeat in gameplay. A saved draft or preview is not a built ROM.

chapters.title: Identify the ROM and its exact revision
chapters.intro: A system header, an exact hash match and a successful playtest answer different questions. Read each result before selecting a named game edit.
steps: Select the imported source and open Resources. Read ROM health & revision and the investigation summary. A filename is a hint, not a verified identity.
For a known reference, use Identify ROM revision. Import your offline CSV, TSV, JSON or XML DAT catalog and select whole-file or supported cartridge-payload scope.
Compare CRC32, SHA-1 or SHA-256 with an expected value for that same scope. Check the region, revision and any copier/header prefix. A mismatch is against the selected reference.
Use Check project on Overview for missing files, stale definitions, overlaps and declared pointer/allocation problems. Recheck after repairing the reported location.
chapters.result: A catalog match identifies exact referenced bytes. Unknown means no matching reference was established. It does not prove corruption. A project check reports its declared structural checks.
chapters.note: A valid console checksum does not prove every game-specific check passes. Hashes do not prove that an edit is fun, balanced or safe in every scene.

details.title: Three separate checks
details.text: Identity: compare measured bytes with an expected revision. Structure: validate supported headers, declared sizes and integrity fields. Behavior: playtest and replay explicit assertions. Keep these conclusions separate.

details.title: Headers and byte scope
details.text: A SNES copier prefix or an NES trainer/header can change file positions and whole-file hashes. Compare a payload reference only with the matching supported payload scope. Never force a named definition onto a close-looking revision.

chapters.caption: Expected 00000000 was entered solely to demonstrate this warning. Compare the measured CRC with a trusted reference for the same byte scope; do not replace it with a convenient value just to clear the warning.

chapters.title: Save drafts, undo and create a build
chapters.intro: Editing changes the proposal shown in the editor. A build is a separate playable output created from a reviewed plan.
steps: Watch the Saving or Saved status as you work. Ctrl+S requests draft saving. A saved draft still needs review and a build.
Use the active editor's Undo and Redo controls. Pixel and room editors group a stroke; text fields retain ordinary text editing undo. The shortcut help explains the current context.
Choose Review changes or the tool's equivalent. Read expected original bytes, proposed values, shared consumers and any integrity updates. Changing an input invalidates an older review.
Create the separate build, select it in the top bar and reload it in Playtest. Compare the intended change and one nearby unchanged behavior.
chapters.result: The source remains intact, the build has its own identity, and the selected Playtest file is the output you just created.
chapters.note: If saving fails, keep the window open and copy unsaved text before reloading. Undoing staged work does not erase a previously created build.

details.title: Draft versus plan
details.text: Drafts hold editor values and staged changes. A plan binds exact changes and preconditions to a source identity. Re-review when the source, definition or staged values change.

details.title: Returning to earlier work
details.text: Use Overview > Build history to inspect versions and meaningful names. Select an earlier output when comparing behavior. Make a complete private project backup before moving work or changing a complex definition.

chapters.caption: Saved means the editing draft is saved. Staged changes still require review and a separate build. An existing build remains available even after an editor undo.

chapters.title: Playtest, pause and save a state
steps: Check that the top selector shows your build, then open Playtest and click Load game.
Choose Play and focus the game for controller input. Use Pause before inspecting a frame. Controller & frame tools exposes manual stepping and input devices.
Choose Save state. Select a saved state and click Load state to return to it. Ordinary battery saves are managed separately below.

chapters.note: Save states are bound to the exact ROM, engine and runtime setup. Do not assume a state from the original will load on a modified build. Loading refreshes one paused frame.

chapters.title: Keep battery saves and states separate
chapters.intro: A battery save is persistent game data such as raw .sav or .srm RAM. A save state captures an emulator session and has much tighter compatibility requirements.
steps: For a snapshot, use Save state beside Play. Select the timestamped state for the same ROM, core and setup, then use Load state. Loading refreshes one paused frame.
For ordinary progress, load the exact game and open Battery saves. Back up the currently exposed save RAM before importing or restarting.
Import raw save data only at the exact supported size. Keep a downloaded backup. Use the game's own load/save menu to confirm progress after a restart.
Use Restart with selected save only after reviewing the chosen file and automatic backup. Keep separate progress for experiments until the edited build is validated.
chapters.result: The selected data has the expected size and identity, a backup exists, and the game can load the intended progress through its normal save system.
chapters.note: A state from an original can be incompatible with a modified build. Wrapped emulator saves are not automatically raw RAM; use the originating emulator's export tools.

details.title: Binding matters
details.text: States depend on exact ROM bytes, engine build, options and system-file setup. Do not treat a matching game title as compatibility. Battery files can also depend on the game revision and save layout.

details.title: Size or initialization mismatch
details.text: Some games expose a different save size after initialization. A refusal preserves the backup; do not pad, truncate or bypass exact-size checks without a separately understood format.

chapters.title: Export a verified patch
steps: Open Export. Select the exact Original revision and the intended Target build. Add a useful title and notes.
Click Create & independently verify patch. ROMancer reconstructs the target with a separate BPS decoder and checks its identity.
Download the prepared patch. Include the expected original revision and instructions with your release, then test applying that patch to a fresh source copy.
chapters.result: The capture follows a successful patch preparation from the modified Chrono Trigger build.
chapters.note: A patch is not a full ROM. BPS checks compatibility using embedded checksums; IPS needs an external source reference. A verified patch proves reconstruction, not complete gameplay correctness. To apply a downloaded patch, use Export > Apply a downloaded patch on the exact original. BPS carries checksums; IPS requires the author's full-file CRC32 or SHA-256 reference. Preview compatibility before creating its separate build.
chapters.intro: Share the verified difference between an exact original and a completed build. State the required source revision with your instructions.
chapters.caption: Actual ROMancer interface. The HTML edition links to the full-resolution capture.

chapters.title: Apply a downloaded BPS or IPS patch safely
chapters.kicker: Exact source / compatibility preview / separate build
chapters.intro: A patch describes a change to a particular source. A matching game title alone is insufficient.
steps: Read the patch author's required region, revision and header treatment. Import your own original into a project and select that original in the top bar; then open Export.

Under Apply a downloaded patch, choose or drop one BPS or IPS file. For IPS, enter the author's full-file reference: eight hexadecimal CRC32 digits or 64 SHA-256 digits. BPS checks embedded checksums.
Choose Preview patch. Read the format, target size and changed-byte count. Expand Changed ranges and identities for source/target hashes and offsets. A zero-change result has nothing to build.
If the reference mismatches, stop and find the required original. Do not remove a header, edit a checksum, or substitute another revision merely to bypass the failure.
Give the output a useful name and choose Create patched build. ROMancer selects the separate output and opens Playtest. Load the game, verify the intended change, and preserve the original.
chapters.result: The pictured BPS was exported from the first-edit exercise. Preview found one changed byte; the 292-byte patch recreated exactly the same SHA-256 as the native-tested asset build.
chapters.note: Changing the selected file can restore its previous editor. Select the original first, then open Export. A valid patch reconstruction establishes bytes, not whole-game behavior. Chain patches only when the next patch explicitly requires the previous output. Patch size includes metadata; sparse runs and dense edits can encode differently. Export does not promise the smallest possible patch.

chapters.title: Check a ROM hack before sharing it
chapters.intro: Use this checklist for the output you intend to distribute. Keep tested observations separate from unknown behavior.
steps: On Overview, run Check project. Resolve errors, read warnings and verify the selected original/build identities. A validation pass covers declared formats, not every gameplay path.
Reload the final build in Playtest. Test the intended change and one nearby behavior that should remain unchanged. Check input and any relevant save/load behavior on this exact build.
For repeatable checks, record routes and screenshot regions. Read Original, Build and Difference results. State which routes and conditions were actually tested.

In Export, create and independently verify the final patch. Confirm the required original revision and full-file hash. Apply the downloaded patch to an unchanged source and compare the reconstructed target hash.

Review Release selection before packaging exports. Only approved patch/document roles enter that package. Keep private project backups, ROM images, saves, captures and personal reports out of the shared selection.

Keep a complete private backup and write clear instructions: required original, patch order if any, expected target identity, intended changes and known limits. Perform a final hands-on trial before announcing success.
chapters.result: A reproducible patch and instructions linked to the exact tested build, with a recovery copy kept separately.
chapters.note: Passing a route or reconstruction check does not certify an entire game. For ROMancer itself, automated release checks are recorded separately; independent human usability feedback still requires a person.

chapters.title: Back up, restore and recover a project
chapters.intro: A project backup is for your own recovery or migration. A public patch package has a different purpose and contains a different selection of data.
steps: Open Projects to choose the right project before editing. Use a separate project for unrelated games or experiments you want to manage independently.
In Settings, make a complete private project backup before moving a workspace or making broad changes. Store the archive outside the working project and confirm it was created.
Restore into the destination workspace, open the recovered project and run Check project. Inspect sources, builds, definitions, drafts and prepared exports.
To remove an unwanted project from the active list, choose Delete project, then Move to Trash. Recover it through Projects > Trash > Restore.
chapters.result: A restored project opens with its owned source and build data. Deleting a project moves its owned files to Trash; the original external ROM stays where it was.
chapters.note: A private backup can contain your ROMs, saves and personal work. Review what you share. Recovery does not make historical reports into fresh native evidence.

details.title: Before cleanup
details.text: Check the project name and current workspace. Keep an independent backup before deleting old application folders or moving manually managed data. A reversible application rollback is not a project backup.

details.title: After restore
details.text: Run fresh native checks before using restored captures or reports as current proof. If a lock blocks recovery, establish that the previous owner process is no longer running; never break an active writer's lock.

chapters.caption: The restoration was checked in this private test workspace. Delete project affects the project-owned copies; an external source ROM is preserved.

chapters.title: Load a mod and compare the changed bytes
chapters.intro: Compare two files in the same project. A patch can create a separate modified build, while a supplied modded ROM can be imported as another source.
steps: Import your original ROM into a project. For a modded ROM file, use Import source in that same project. For BPS/IPS, select the original and open Export > Apply a downloaded patch. IPS requires the author’s original CRC32 or SHA-256 reference.

Choose Preview patch, inspect the changed-byte count and source identity, then Create patched build. The original remains unchanged. A successful BPS reconstruction does not establish each changed byte’s gameplay meaning.

Open Overview > Build history > Compare files. Choose the original/earlier file and the modified/later file, then click Compare files. Read the full changed-byte count and select a listed changed range.

In Resources, compare Earlier bytes and Selected bytes. Highlights mark differences. A dash means that file has no byte at that offset. Use the comparison page controls for added/removed regions, or Follow hex editor to use its current position.

chapters.note: A shifted or recompressed resource can change many bytes without creating many separate gameplay changes. The range list can be truncated; its changed-byte total still covers the complete comparison. File-relative differences do not prove that offsets mean the same thing after relocation.

chapters.title: Inspect bytes with useful context
steps: Use a Known locations > View 0x... button to jump to a documented offset, or open Resources and enter an offset.
Search bytes such as AB ?? CD, UTF-8 text or an integer with explicit byte order. Inspect signed/unsigned numbers, read nearby verified notes and bookmark the selected offset before editing.
Edit a byte using two hex digits. Choose Review byte edits, inspect the plan, then Create separate build.
chapters.result: The editor is opened at The Immortal's documented menu bytes rather than an arbitrary location.
chapters.note: Hexadecimal is a way to write numbers; it does not tell you what a byte means. Unknown data stays unknown until evidence establishes its structure and purpose.
chapters.intro: Inspect exact stored bytes with a known purpose and an explicit address scope. Use higher-level tools when their definitions describe the change.

chapters.title: Trace a declared range to the exact bytes
chapters.intro: Follow a named room, object field, table or sound range into the selected source. Explanations describe established encodings and declared relationships, while unknown byte purposes remain unknown.
steps: In Resources, open Declared resource catalog, choose Index declared resources and search a name. Checked definitions can expose rooms, object slots, table ranges, samples and songs. Use Inspect on the intended range.

Select a byte in the hex editor. Open Number inspector & bookmarks, then Explain selected bytes. Read its source-bound name, offset, stored bytes, numeric value, byte order and declared bounds when available.

For room data, compare the cell X/Y or object slot and field. For a mapped exit field, read the declared destination. Use Declared resource relationships to follow named source ranges; these relationships do not establish arbitrary code references.

In Troubleshooting, use Find declared references or Resolve address, then Inspect mapped bytes. Confirm the current source, mapping and bank. Recompute after switching sources; do not reuse a stale result.
chapters.result: The hex selection belongs to the intended artifact and declared file offset. The explanation identifies its bounded stored meaning, or explicitly reports that no interpretation has been established.
chapters.note: A declared room target is not a measured traversal. Raw collision values are not inferred walkability labels. Sound samples and identified sequence fields do not establish an unknown commercial driver, and imported traces do not establish native instruction events.

details.title: What a declaration can explain
details.text: A terrain/collision cell can identify its room and coordinates; an object field can identify the named slot, value and declared target. Metatile parts, table fields, samples and supported song events retain their own range and format context.

details.title: Use the matching kind of tool
details.text: A source editor changes checked stored data. A game-authoring engine needs its own executable runtime and event system. Instruction breakpoints require a real CPU-debugging adapter. The current investigation tools provide byte comparisons and bounded observations, not a full instruction debugger.

details.title: Protect the selected context
details.text: Reference jumps, mapped-address inspection and memory watches belong to a source/runtime context. Re-selecting a file, build or session requires a fresh compatible observation. A changed RAM value alone does not identify a ROM address or the instruction that wrote it.

notes.text: This capture selects 0x3515 and explains the Hillside / Courtyard connection / x field as an 8-bit declared value of 12, bounded from 0 to 15. The separate byte-reference panel correctly does not claim verified game semantics.

notes.title: Drafts and source bytes differ
notes.text: An inspector can show a staged X position of 13 while the selected original source still stores 12. Create and select the separate build before expecting a byte explanation to describe that built edit.

notes.title: Keep navigation current
notes.text: Go selects the visible byte cursor. After moving or switching sources, request the explanation again. A previous number interpretation or reference result does not describe a newly selected byte automatically.

chapters.title: Discover resources and declare a format
chapters.intro: Offline investigation can identify known revisions and suggest possible structures. A candidate is a lead to inspect, not permission to edit arbitrary bytes.
steps: Read the automatic investigation after import. Keep exact known identities separate from candidate text, graphics, pointer or compression matches.
Use Rescan ROM for changed data or Find resources for a focused byte range. Read any partial-range report and continue the next range when needed.
Confirm the offset, format, dimensions, allocation and source identity before declaring a resource. Inspect surrounding bytes and independent references for the exact revision.
Save the checked definition. Reopen it on the same source and compare the preview with a measured game scene before applying edits.
chapters.result: The editor decodes the intended resource from bounded, explicitly identified storage. A later build must meet the same source and original-byte preconditions.
chapters.note: A plausible picture or readable word can occur inside code or unrelated data. Automatic discovery cannot establish arbitrary enemy names, animation scripts or sound-driver commands.

details.title: System formats
details.text: NES stored CHR uses planar 2bpp; Game Boy uses paired row bitplanes. SNES templates support paired 4bpp; Genesis supports packed 4bpp and big-endian palette words. GBA templates include low-nibble-first 4bpp and RGB555. Each game can add compression and its own layout.

details.title: Six supported modes
details.text: NES, SNES, Genesis, GB, GBC and GBA are separate user choices. Bank switching, enhancement hardware and game-specific data need their own supported mapping or verified definition. Unknown bytes remain inspectable, with editing or execution refused when support is not established. The declared catalog also exposes checked level and sound ranges; it does not discover arbitrary room identities or music-driver commands.

details.title: Automatic versus manual investigation
details.text: Settings enables Auto deep scan on ROM load by default. You can choose a manual scan instead. Automatic paused-gameplay graphics analysis examines available observed data; its candidates still need format and ownership confirmation.

chapters.title: Paint an assembled sprite
steps: Open Graphics & fonts. With verified or declared tiles loaded, use Sprite assembly to arrange the parts.
Choose a brush color index and paint in Editing - paint here. Compare the fixed Original image with the edited preview.
Use Undo sprite stroke or Redo sprite stroke, then Review asset changes and create a build.
chapters.result: The capture shows an actual changed pixel on a 16 x 32 Simon assembly made from eight tiles.
chapters.note: This example uses a declared tile layout and observed gameplay colors. It does not prove automatic sprite assembly for every game. Preview colors do not change palette bytes.
chapters.intro: An explicit assembly places known tiles into a useful sprite view. Painting edits the referenced tiles; the arrangement itself does not discover game logic.
chapters.caption: Actual ROMancer interface. The HTML edition links to the full-resolution capture.

chapters.title: Edit stored palette entries deliberately
chapters.intro: A pixel usually stores a color index. A palette supplies the RGB color for that index. Changing the palette can recolor many uses at once.
steps: Load a declared graphics resource and inspect Palette colors. Select the bank and entry before editing. Confirm the original swatch matches the intended resource.
Use Choose color for an RGB proposal, or Color storage values for the declared channels. Read the Original/Edited comparison as the change is staged.
Review the channel limits and shared consumers. RGB555 stores 5-bit channels, so a chosen screen color is quantized to a representable value.
Review asset changes, create the build and inspect every scene known to share that palette. Verify the color in the actual game, not just the swatch.
chapters.result: The proposed color is representable in the declared format; the build changes the intended palette bytes and the scene uses them as expected.
chapters.note: Preview colors used to arrange a sprite are not necessarily stored palette edits. Transparency, banks and a game's dynamic palette changes can affect the observed result.

details.title: Shared entries
details.text: One index can be referenced by multiple tiles, objects or frames. A correct local swatch can cause an unintended global recolor. Inspect declared consumers and compare an unchanged neighboring object.

details.title: Original versus edited
details.text: The original view remains the reference while the edited view follows staged values. Saving the editor draft does not modify the playable source. Build and reload before judging the in-game effect.

chapters.caption: Application themes and stored game palettes are separate. Review the decoded color preview, shared uses and proposed bytes, then playtest the scene in the new build.

visual_page.title: Compare palette colors before building
visual_page.intro: The Wario Land 4 example shows an exact-revision palette change in the editor and the resulting visual preview.

panels.title: Compare palette colors before building
panels.caption: Application themes and stored game palettes are separate. Review the decoded color preview, shared uses and proposed bytes, then playtest the scene in the new build.

chapters.title: Preview an explicitly assembled animation
chapters.intro: Animation frames let you compare declared arrangements over time. They do not automatically identify or rewrite a commercial game's animation script.
steps: Arrange the tiles for one frame in Sprite assembly. Open Animation frames, set Frame duration (ms) and choose Add assembled frame.
Create the other explicit frame arrangements. Select a frame to inspect it, use Edit selected frame to revise its layout, or Remove selected frame to remove it from this preview.
Use Play animation and Pause animation to review the proposed sequence. Read the shared-tile count before changing pixels.
Review the actual asset changes and build them. Playtest the real game animation to establish whether its own script uses the edited tiles in the intended order.
chapters.result: The preview cycles through the layouts you supplied and reflects staged tile/palette edits. The unchanged original remains available for comparison.
chapters.note: Editing a tile reused across frames changes every preview frame that references it. A timing value in this preview is not proof of the game's stored animation timing.

details.title: What is saved
details.text: The frame list is an explicit editor layout. Only supported reviewed asset changes become ROM bytes. Keep resource definitions and game-specific script evidence separate.

details.title: Useful first check
details.text: Make a one-pixel change in one tile, find every frame that shares it, then undo. This reveals the practical reach of a tile before you commit a larger redraw.

chapters.title: Paint a declared tilemap
chapters.intro: A tilemap is a grid of references to tiles. Entries can also contain palette banks or horizontal and vertical flip flags, depending on the declared format.
steps: Inspect a graphics definition that includes the tilemap location, dimensions, entry format and associated tile/palette resources. Confirm the original map preview.
Select the map brush or entry and stage the intended tile index, palette bank and flip values. Compare the map preview while keeping the original as the reference.
Use the tilemap editor's supported painting tools and undo controls for bounded strokes. For a specific entry, inspect its stored values before staging a change.
Review asset changes and shared consumers. Create a build and load the game location that uses the map, including scrolling or transitions that might load other banks.
chapters.result: The reviewed map entry references a valid tile and allowed bank/flip values. The rendered game screen shows the intended arrangement.
chapters.note: A tilemap is a display arrangement. Collision, objects and exits can live in separate records and will not automatically follow a visual change.

details.title: PNG import
details.text: For supported graphics imports, choose exact palette mapping or explicitly review nearest-color conversion. Importing artwork does not establish the ROM's resource location or capacity.

details.title: Reuse matters
details.text: A tile edit changes every map entry that reuses that tile. A map-entry edit changes its reference instead. Pick the operation that matches the intended scope.

chapters.title: Rebalance named equipment and enemy stats
steps: In Overview > Game edits, open the desired attack, armor, helm, base-price or enemy-stat table. The original attack-only resource ID remains compatible with older definitions.
Search by name or ID, choose the record, and select Show selected record. Edit only the exposed numeric fields. The Original/Edited preview updates as you type.

Keep critical rates within 0 to 100. HP and prices use the declared integer widths; batch changes refuse numeric overflow and field-limit violations. Blank or unused slots are not promises of gameplay content.
Choose Review changes, inspect the exact records, then Create build. Playtest the new build. Stored attack, defense and prices can be transformed by game formulas or battle scripts.
chapters.result: A named record receives a checked fixed-width edit. The screenshot shows a real armor record and its changed defense preview.
chapters.note: The current definitions cover 85 weapon slots (74 named), 32 named armor slots, 24 named helms and 251 enemy slots (212 named). Effects, flags, rewards and scripts are preserved. These counts describe the exact original, not every external hack. For other games, table layouts still require a verified definition.
chapters.intro: The exact USA Chrono Trigger profile supplies named equipment and enemy tables. Names are decoded from your selected ROM, with record IDs kept beside duplicates and blank slots.

chapters.title: Translate through CSV or TSV
chapters.intro: The translation spreadsheet preserves the source text and stable record identity. Edit the translation column while keeping the exported structure intact.
steps: Inspect editable text in Text & layout. Open Translation spreadsheet and download CSV or TSV for the selected source and definition.
Keep every stable ID, original-text field and control column. Edit only translation. Preserve delimiters, quoted multiline fields and the same file format when saving.
Import the sheet back into the same source context. Review unmapped characters, protected controls and encoded byte capacity for each changed record.
Preview the translation plan, create a separate build and test menus, dialogue, line breaks and transitions using the actual font and game logic.
chapters.result: Changed rows map back to the exported records. Original controls are protected and every translation fits its declared encoding and allocation.
chapters.note: Character count and encoded byte count can differ. A spreadsheet that silently reformats IDs or line breaks can invalidate the import. Shorten text or correct an established allocation rather than bypassing limits.

details.title: A useful first round-trip
details.text: Export a sheet, change one short line and reimport it before translating hundreds of rows. Keep the original export as a reference and a project backup outside the workspace.

details.title: Text preview limits
details.text: A system-font comparison helps review wording. It does not establish glyph availability, game-window width or dialogue behavior. Use declared font/layout measurements and native playtesting for those checks.

chapters.title: Declare text, fonts and layout limits
chapters.intro: Text bytes need an encoding and storage layout. Font and window measurements add useful checks when those formats are explicitly declared.
steps: Declare the text offset, slot capacity, encoding and terminator, or load a verified definition for the exact source. Add pointer information only when its location and mapping are established.
Inspect records and visible control tokens. Edit wording while preserving required controls and segment boundaries. Read capacity and unmapped-character feedback.
For declared fonts and menu/dialogue layouts, inspect the actual decoded-font canvas, glyph metrics and available dimensions. Treat a measured overflow as a concrete issue in that declared layout.
Review the exact plan, including pointer or integrity changes, build and test the actual screen. Inspect the following record or menu item for unintended damage.
chapters.result: The edited record fits the supported allocation, preserves protected bytes and displays correctly in the tested game window.
chapters.note: An offset is not a CPU address. A linear pointer base does not establish a bank-switched mapping. A fixed slot cannot grow just because more words fit in the editor.

details.title: Control codes
details.text: Commands can change colors, insert names, wait for input or end a record. Preserve their declared structure even when they look like punctuation or empty bytes.

details.title: Fonts and graphics
details.text: Glyph painting uses declared graphics storage. Changing a glyph can affect every string that uses it. A layout measurement covers its supplied font and dimensions, not every screen in the game.

chapters.title: Edit declared terrain, objects and collision
chapters.intro: Levels needs a checked game-specific definition. The matched FFL II bedroom is a bounded real-game example. An unsupported source has no level definition; optional Advanced practice teaches the declared format without pretending to decode that game.
steps: Open Levels for the selected source. If it says No supported level map for this ROM yet, investigate the source or supply a checked map definition through Advanced level setup. The separate collapsed Advanced practice > Open test layout is a learning exercise, not your game.

Choose Room and Paint layer: Terrain or declared Collision values. Select a Terrain brushes thumbnail, or use Pick from room to sample a cell. Compare Original room with the editing canvas; paint, fill or select/copy/paste within the declared grid.

Use Undo stroke and Redo stroke. With Named objects and Move object, select or drag a named label. Use Objects > Update preview for a declared destination. Raw coordinates and fields stay inside Position & advanced values; unnamed slots require All records (Advanced).
Choose Review level changes, inspect the exact changes, then Create level build. Visit the room and test walking, collision, boundaries and transitions.
chapters.result: Changed grid/object fields stay within the declared ranges. The game renders the room, moves through it and follows the intended transitions.
chapters.note: Visual terrain does not establish collision semantics. Collision values are raw stored data. Only declared names appear by default; raw slot kinds and records stay Advanced. Named roles do not establish native actors or doors, and the practice layout is not an executable game-authoring workflow.

details.title: Shared metatiles
details.text: A block can be used in many cells or rooms. Changing its component tile changes every declared use; changing one terrain cell selects a different block for that cell.

details.title: Optional practice is not your game
details.text: The artificial Hillside/Courtyard layouts demonstrate checked storage and declared relationships. Only Hillside graphics and music are rendered by the native test program. Their other room, objects and connections are editor practice data, not implemented doors or events. Actual game-room editing requires a verified definition for that game and revision.

chapters.title: Advanced practice: objects and room connections
chapters.intro: This optional Advanced practice uses original synthetic test terrain and declared records to demonstrate the editor format. It is not a decoded commercial-game level. For an actual supported game-room edit, start with the matched Final Fantasy Legend II bedroom example.
steps: Open Advanced practice > Open test layout only to learn the declared format. Read the Practice layout warning. Under Choose a room, choose Hillside or Courtyard: these are synthetic test layouts, not decoded commercial levels.
Keep Named objects selected in Overlay. Select a named map label or use Selected object under Objects. Choose Move object and drag its label within the guarded room bounds.
For a declared exit, select Destination room and choose Update preview. Exact X/Y and raw fields are inside Position & advanced values. Unnamed raw slots appear only with All records (Advanced).

Inspect the staged room link, follow its destination button and use Undo stroke to undo a grouped edit. Review and build only the intended stored changes; the workshop's room links and records still do not run as gameplay.
chapters.result: The practice inspector stages bounded declared fields, and editor navigation follows an explicit stored-value mapping. These checks demonstrate data handling, not an executable level or door system.
chapters.note: This is editor-format practice, not normal beginner game editing. The native test program renders Hillside and plays music only. Courtyard, object records and declared connections are not executed as actors, doors or events. Use the real FFL II bedroom example for a native-supported room edit.

details.title: What a connection declares
details.text: An optional per-slot annotation supplies its index, name and role. A declared exit names a stored integer field and lists allowed value/room-ID pairs. Unmapped current values, duplicate destination values, unknown rooms and out-of-range edits are rejected.

details.title: Existing definitions still work
details.text: The optional object metadata does not replace the fixed-record storage layout or require a new schema version. Older definitions remain usable; unnamed slots stay unnamed, and objects without established X/Y coordinates are not given invented positions.

details.title: Workshop versus game engine
details.text: Hillside and Courtyard demonstrate source-bound layouts, named fields and declared navigation in the editor. These data do not provide a game-authoring engine, executable door events or an event compiler. Verify a real game's consumers before claiming an edited destination works in native play.

chapters.title: Preview sound and respect driver limits
chapters.intro: Console audio hardware and a game's music driver are different layers. Native audio recording can work even when sequence editing is unavailable.
steps: Open Music & sound. Read the hardware information and Music driver status. Unknown driver means sequence editing is unavailable.
For actual game output, load the source in Playtest, reach the sound, then use Record native preview. Play, pause, seek or loop the resulting preview and save a WAV when useful.

For a supported sample, use a verified offset, allocation, codec and preview sample rate. Choose Check declared sample, then preview gain, reverse, silence or supported WAV replacement before staging. Staged edits update Original and Edited PCM waveform previews; use their play controls when ready. Audio does not autoplay.
Review sound changes, create a sound build and test the real scene. Use note/event or transpose operations only when a supported sequence definition is identified.
chapters.result: The decoded preview corresponds to the intended declared sample, and the game plays the built result at the expected rate and without an unintended neighboring change.
chapters.note: A valid codec does not locate a sample or determine its rate, loop or instrument. Lossy re-encoding can change sound quality. A synthesized sequence preview does not certify the native driver result. Supported sequence editing is available in the workshop definition; that does not establish a commercial game driver.

details.title: Two preview paths
details.text: Native recording captures the engine's mixed output for the selected game session. A declared sample preview decodes a bounded stored resource. They answer different questions and can sound different.

details.title: When music cannot be edited
details.text: Keep unknown driver data unchanged. Use native recording, document the observed scene and find evidence for the exact driver and revision. Do not invent note commands from a console hardware label.

chapters.caption: This capture demonstrates a supported NES DPCM sample and an original practice definition. It does not establish the driver, sample locations or music commands of a commercial game.

chapters.title: Extract and reinsert supported compression
chapters.intro: A decoded resource is not automatically safe to write back at a new size. Recompression must fit an established parent allocation.
steps: Select a validated supported LZ10 or RLE stream in Resources. Confirm its codec, file offset and allocated capacity using evidence for this revision.
Extract the decoded resource into the project. Inspect and edit it through the normal supported editors, then create the edited decoded build.
Select that edited decoded build and review recompression into its original parent. Read the proposed compressed length and confirmed capacity.
Create the parent build only when the stream fits. Inspect the independently decoded comparison, then playtest the actual game resource.
chapters.result: The encoded stream fits without overwriting neighbors, and independent decoding reconstructs every intended decoded byte.
chapters.note: Unrecognized compression remains read-only. A run of zeroes or another fill pattern does not establish unowned capacity. Do not increase an allocation or move a stream to clear an error without a separately supported ownership and pointer model. Recompression is checked by the primary decoder and a separate original token parser; this is implementation diversity, not independent emulator certification.

details.title: Parent and child
details.text: Extraction creates a resource with an explicit relationship to its parent bytes. Editing a child does not automatically modify the game. Reinsert the selected child build and test the resulting parent ROM.

details.title: Capacity and relocation limits
details.text: Recompression stays inside its declared parent allocation. The separate Advanced data-move workflow checks explicitly declared linear references and reserved space; it does not discover compressed-stream ownership or make an oversized reinsertion safe. Follow the data-relocation chapter rather than increasing capacity to silence a failure.

chapters.title: Record routes and compare builds
chapters.intro: A regression route repeats explicit inputs and checks an expected observation. Define what should remain unchanged and what is intentionally different.
steps: Open Routes and start recording controller inputs. Reach the screen in Playtest, pause and capture a measured frame for the selected build.
In Screenshot checkpoints, select a stable region up to 256 x 256 pixels. Add the checkpoint to the latest recorded input, then stop and save the recording.
Replay the recorded checkpoint. For original/build comparison, save a cold-start definition, open Regression, select the original, build and up to eight routes, then run the suite.
Read baseline, build and assertion results separately. Inspect expected, actual and difference images on a failure. Rerun after fixing a relevant change.
chapters.result: The baseline passes its defined assertions before the build is evaluated. Results are bound to the measured source, engine and route setup.
chapters.note: A passing region or route covers that observation. It does not certify the entire game. Timing, random state, blinking or scrolling can make an unsuitable screenshot reference unstable.

details.title: Choose assertions deliberately
details.text: For a palette edit, capture the changed interface and an unchanged scene. For a balance edit, compare the stored value and a repeatable in-game action. A detected intentional difference can be expected.

details.title: Smoke checks
details.text: Check ROM runs a short 120-frame fresh-worker test and measures output. It can establish startup evidence, but it is not a campaign test, a save-system test or a substitute for explicit expected gameplay.

details.title: Progression coverage
details.text: Routes also expose Progression coverage. Select authenticated route records and declare required, optional, ending and unknown objectives, then build the coverage graph. Unvisited objectives stay separate; imported PASS labels do not grant coverage. An advanced declared resource model states supplied action costs and assumptions rather than inferring combat rules.

chapters.title: Inspect memory and translate addresses
chapters.intro: File offsets, console addresses and emulator memory regions describe different spaces. Declare the mapping before comparing or editing them.
steps: Start with exact source/build bytes and a known offset. Use the number inspector to choose signedness and byte order rather than guessing from a displayed decimal value.

In Address explorer, choose the supported Declared mapping and required bank/bounds, then Resolve address. Use Inspect mapped bytes to open that current source location. An active hardware bank is not observed by this declaration.

Load a matching Playtest session. Under Find a changing value, use Start RAM search, play one action, pause, then Capture & narrow by changed, unchanged, increased, decreased or exact value. Add a watch to a measured result.

Use the native capture workflow for actual access events. Declared mappings, imported traces and changed RAM values remain separate evidence types. The recorded context is a lead, not proof of game meaning or DMA ownership.
chapters.result: The translated location uses the intended mapping and bank. A watch reports the selected memory value for the actual loaded session.
chapters.note: A changed value does not identify the instruction that wrote it. A byte pattern match is not proof that the same code or structure exists in a different revision.

details.title: Tables and pointers
details.text: For a declared linear table pointer, target file offset = stored value - base. Record stride is the distance between entries; a field offset is relative to each record. Bank switching needs additional mapping evidence. Find declared references follows only supplied mappings; undeclared code uses remain unknown.

details.title: Memory is not a ROM location
details.text: RAM matches do not identify the stored ROM source of a value. Available video-memory previews decode exposed bytes as indexed grayscale tiles; palette, object attributes and ROM ownership remain unknown. Use repeated controlled observations to narrow a candidate.

chapters.title: Reuse checked recipes and definitions
chapters.intro: A recipe repeats supported source-bound operations. A definition describes storage. Neither import grants arbitrary shell execution or native evidence trust.
steps: Open More tools > Recipes & definitions and select the exact original source revision.
After reviewing or building edits, use Save a plan as a recipe, or import an existing recipe JSON file. Keep the recipe with its source identity and intended purpose.
Preview every operation and affected range on rerun. Resolve wrong hashes, overlaps and unsupported commands before creating a new build.

Export checked Text, Graphics & fonts, Data tables, Levels & objects or Music & sound definitions in Resource definitions. Reimport the JSON on the same source, choose Check and import definition and inspect the decoded result before editing.
chapters.result: The recipe produces a fresh reviewable plan for the exact source and rejects stale or incompatible assumptions. The new build remains separate.
chapters.note: A recipe from a trusted person can still target a different revision. Inspect the plan rather than treating the filename or previous success as authority.

details.title: Batch table changes
details.text: The table editor previews up to 1,024 source records. Choose set, add, multiply or percent, then inspect the range. Percent changes round halves away from zero; numeric overflow is refused. Game-specific limits still require evidence.

details.title: Checked definition exchange
details.text: The exported envelope records source SHA-256 and size, resource kind and checked definition. Level object metadata and sound layouts travel as declarations, not runtime proof. Wrong sources or invalid definitions refuse; ROM files and native reports are excluded. Existing version-1 definitions keep their format.

chapters.title: Use AI and MCP with explicit permissions
chapters.intro: ROMancer works without AI. Compatible clients can use its local MCP stdio adapter to inspect supported data and, when explicitly enabled, create checked builds.
steps: Open Settings > AI & LLM access to create a client configuration with the correct interpreter and workspace. The root README documents the command-line entry point.
Start with read-only access. The source entry point is python -B -m romancer.mcp_server --workspace <workspace-folder>. Use the installed interpreter for the bundled edition.
Enable writes with --allow-writes only for a deliberate editing session. Add --rom-root <folder> for each dedicated folder from which that client may import ROMs.
Require the same inspect, plan, build, playtest and patch-verification cycle. Review generated plans and sharing content yourself. Keep ROMs, save data and personal paths private.
chapters.result: The client uses structured supported operations against the intended workspace. Read-only mode refuses writes, and imported sources stay within explicitly allowed roots.
chapters.note: MCP is an optional transport, not a built-in model or proof of game semantics. Source identity, numeric budgets, current runtime context and read/write permissions still apply to each structured call.

details.title: Bounded investigation operations
details.text: The exposed tools include explicit address resolution, declared references, bounded byte explanations, memory searches and watches, exposed video-tile inspection and supported compression checks. Use the client's available-tool list and input schemas first. system.operations describes backend operations; some are not exposed through MCP. Some observations create temporary search state or saved ranges and therefore require write-enabled access; they do not write arbitrary native RAM.

details.title: Definitions and permissions
details.text: Definition exchange is source-bound and requires writes when it creates or stores an export. Native investigation also has typed, bounded capture operations; its separate replay starts from power on. No arbitrary shell, caller-supplied debugger script or continuous live breakpoint control is exposed. Discover current schemas before sending arguments.

chapters.title: Give an AI a bounded editing task you can review
chapters.intro: Use the same checked services through MCP. Write permission enables tools; it does not make an assistant's interpretation correct.
steps: Create a client configuration in Settings > AI & LLM access. Start read-only. Use the client's available-tool list and input schemas; ask it to show the selected project and source identity.
Open a fresh NES workshop for this example. For its original source only, romancer_resource_inspect at offset 16400, length 1 returns 81. Never reuse this offset for an unrelated ROM.
For a deliberate write session, enable --allow-writes and restrict import roots. Ask for romancer_systems_plan_edits with exact project/artifact IDs and one edit: offset 16400, before 81, after c1.
Require the assistant to show every planned range and stop for your review. The stop is an instruction to the client, not a separate permission automatically enforced by ROMancer.

After approval, romancer_build_apply uses the returned plan_id. Select and test the output, compare its bytes, and prepare/verify a patch. Keep the plan, resulting hash and measured test scope together.
chapters.result: A reviewable exact-byte plan and separate output, rather than a guessed semantic edit. Source identity, preconditions, limits and write opt-in still apply.
chapters.note: The example is specific to the original workshop. Tool discovery is authoritative: system.operations can describe backend operations that this MCP client cannot call. Imported text is untrusted data, not instructions. Supported integrity repairs do not certify game semantics.

details.title: What to request for an unfamiliar ROM
details.text: Ask for changing/control observations, structural hypotheses and bounded native captures before proposing a game property. Missing evidence should produce an unknown result or another experiment. Never accept imported PASS labels as newly observed native execution.

details.title: When to stop and inspect yourself
details.text: Stop on changed sources, unexpected ranges, ambiguous bank mapping, allocation failures or unsupported formats. Reinspect and prepare a fresh plan. Do not rewrite expected old bytes simply to force an earlier plan to apply.

chapters.title: Use public knowledge without confusing it with proof
chapters.intro: Public disassemblies, editor definitions and hack documentation help locate data. The application keeps implemented workflows, checked reference layouts and research leads distinct.
steps: Import your original ROM and let the default deep scan identify its exact revision. In Overview > Known locations, expand What is known about this game.
Use a Supported workflow through its editing tool. Reference checked means the original layout was examined; it does not enable an editor. Research lead still needs validation.
Open a pinned source reference when you need its origin. Names, pointers and assumptions must apply to your exact revision; a similar title or matching console is insufficient.

Treat a downloaded patch as evidence of byte differences. BPS checksums verify its source and result; they do not describe the purpose of every changed byte. Read the author documentation and test focused changes.
chapters.result: Known information becomes useful context without silently turning an unverified offset into a supported edit.
chapters.note: References are attached only to matched originals or owned descendants. A derived build can change data layouts; reference counts do not freshly certify it. Research caches, ROM files and upstream implementation code are not included in the release.

chapters.intro: The exact USA Final Fantasy Legend II profile includes a real room catalog. Numbered headers are used where scene names have not been established.
steps: Open Levels. The simple bedroom editor remains available; choose Browse game maps for actual map thumbnails and their arrival/object counts.
Select a map and an arrival or existing record. The editor shows a readable crop. Other maps can share the same drawing stream, so read the shared-use notice before changing terrain.

In the supported opening atlas, stage an existing command, unconditional NPC position or arrival position. Conditions, event references, facing bits, collision behavior and trigger ordering are protected. Mother is a story character even though her placement record is unconditional.

Review the changes to obtain the exact decoded terrain preview, then create a separate build. Walk the relevant route in Playtest, test interactions and both exits, and save a state only for its matching build.
chapters.result: The selected supported record changes through a source-bound plan, with an original/edited map preview and a separate playable build.
chapters.note: The catalog has 219 header variants and 164 drawing streams. Conditional branches require explicit state; unsupported decoding stays unavailable. Non-opening maps use clearly marked neutral color-index previews until a native palette is known. Object records are not a claim that every object is visible in the current game state. chapters.title: Find the cause before repeating a change
chapters.intro: Read the reported source, location and failed precondition. A useful next step reduces uncertainty instead of applying the same edit repeatedly.
steps: If the game did not change, check the selected source/build, Saved status and whether a build was created. Reload the new build in Playtest; an old session can still be running.
If a definition or patch refuses, compare exact revision, byte scope and original bytes. For text, inspect controls/encoding/capacity. For graphics, inspect codec, bank and shared consumers.
If playback or sound fails, check the selected system, engine setup, game focus and audio controls. GB and GBC need the right mode. Restore only compatible states and supported raw save data.
Run project checks and Settings > Diagnostics & support. Review the sanitized preview, then download the report if you want to share it. No report is sent automatically.
chapters.result: You have a specific failed condition, a reproducible input and a measured observation. Correct the narrow issue, rerun the relevant check and preserve the earlier backup.
chapters.note: Do not erase originals, bypass identity checks or reinterpret unknown data just to clear an error. A passing later check should address the actual earlier failure.

details.title: Useful support detail
details.text: State the operation, application revision, selected system, expected result and actual result. Review any screenshot or log for personal information before sharing. Sanitized reports exclude ROM/save bytes, credentials, personal paths, project names and raw errors. The three checklists that follow cover identity and patch problems, editing problems, and playback or recovery problems. Each gives a meaning and a next step.

details.title: Recovery order
details.text: Keep unsaved text, back up the project, check the source identity, reproduce one small step, inspect the failure and restore or correct the narrow change. Historical reports are references; run fresh native checks for a current claim. For a room destination or mapped-address issue, inspect its checked definition and exact source bytes before treating the result as runtime behavior.

chapters.title: ROM and patch problems
chapters.intro: Start here when an import, identity check or downloaded patch does not match what you expected.
steps: Confirm which file is selected. A source, a modified build and a header-stripped file can have different hashes even when their names look alike.
Read the expected and measured values, comparison scope and patch instructions. Check the region and revision before trying another source.
If the source is correct and a structural check still fails, preserve it and collect the exact failed check. Obtain another verified dump or a documented explanation before editing.
chapters.result: Repeat the relevant check after the correction. Keep the original, the earlier build and your backup available until the new result is confirmed.
chapters.note: A warning explains a limited check. It is not permission to bypass a failed precondition. If the cause remains unknown, keep that resource unchanged and include the operation and measured result in a reviewed support report.

details.title: CRC32 mismatch
details.text: The measured bytes differ from the entered reference. Confirm whole-file versus payload scope, copier prefix, trainer, region and revision. A blank expected value means no reference comparison was performed, not that the dump matched.

details.title: Unknown game or missing named tools
details.text: A valid system header does not identify a game revision. Import a trusted local hash catalog. Use generic inspection or a separately checked definition; a similar filename or another game's offsets are insufficient.

details.title: BPS source mismatch / IPS has no source checksum
details.text: BPS validates its embedded source identity. Choose the exact source required by the patch. IPS does not supply this proof: check an external source reference and the resulting output rather than treating a successful apply as compatibility.

details.title: Header, size or startup warning
details.text: Read which structure failed. Unusual homebrew headers can produce warnings. Unknown mapper state or an unsupported branch form can be Not checked. Investigate those limits; do not call them successful execution.

details.title: Scan limited or interrupted
details.text: A byte, time or result budget limits that analysis. Review completed findings and the named unavailable part. Retry the bounded operation or inspect a smaller declared range. Increasing a budget does not establish missing game semantics.

chapters.title: Editing and preview problems
chapters.intro: Use these checks when a proposed edit is blocked, a preview looks wrong or the game still shows an older value.
steps: Keep the current text or proposal before reloading. Check the selected source/build and the exact resource definition.
Correct the narrow issue, then request a fresh review. An old plan cannot authorize changed source bytes or a different proposal.
Create a separate build and reload that build in Playtest. Compare the intended scene and one nearby unchanged behavior.
chapters.result: Repeat the relevant check after the correction. Keep the original, the earlier build and your backup available until the new result is confirmed.
chapters.note: A warning explains a limited check. It is not permission to bypass a failed precondition. If the cause remains unknown, keep that resource unchanged and include the operation and measured result in a reviewed support report.

details.title: The edit is saved, but the game did not change
details.text: Saved refers to the draft. Review changes, create a build, select it in the top bar and reload it in Playtest. A preview notification does not mean that playable ROM bytes were written.

details.title: Text too long, unmapped character or damaged spreadsheet
details.text: Use encoded bytes, not character count. Preserve control codes, stable IDs and original columns; edit only translations. Re-export a fresh sheet and try one short row. Shorten text or establish a supported allocation instead of dropping controls.

details.title: Wrong colors, scrambled tiles or shared edits
details.text: Check codec, source bank, stored palette and tile arrangement. Editor preview colors may be metadata rather than palette bytes. Inspect declared shared consumers before approving a change that appears in several frames or rooms.

details.title: Stale definition, changed source or overlapping edits
details.text: Reinspect the exact source and declared ranges. Reuse a parent definition only through its guarded workflow. Reconcile overlaps and dependencies; obtain a fresh plan rather than forcing expected bytes to match.

details.title: Map, animation, audio or compressed resource unavailable
details.text: A system label does not decode a game-specific format. Use only supported definitions. A sample codec does not find instruments, a frame layout does not decode an animation script, and a map preview does not prove collision. Respect compressed allocation limits.

chapters.title: Playback, saving and recovery problems
chapters.intro: Protect progress first. Check the selected output and session before replacing data or restarting.
steps: Preserve unsaved text and download a backup of exposed battery-save RAM before experimenting with imports or restarts.
Confirm the selected ROM, engine, input device, audio controls and save format. Reproduce one small problem at a time.
Use Projects > Trash to restore an accidentally deleted project. Run fresh checks after restore, then review a sanitized support report if the issue persists.
chapters.result: Repeat the relevant check after the correction. Keep the original, the earlier build and your backup available until the new result is confirmed.
chapters.note: A warning explains a limited check. It is not permission to bypass a failed precondition. If the cause remains unknown, keep that resource unchanged and include the operation and measured result in a reviewed support report.

details.title: Application will not finish opening
details.text: Keep the complete portable folder together. Use the supplied launcher or installed shortcut; inspect startup details. Check file access and the local service. Retry after correcting the reported problem. Preserve the workspace when reinstalling.

details.title: No game input or sound
details.text: Load the intended build in Playtest. Select the connected controller/type and give the game focus. Check mute, volume and output controls. An unknown sequence driver does not prevent supported native audio recording.

details.title: Save state refused / battery save has the wrong size
details.text: States require the same ROM bytes, engine and setup. Use the state with its matching output. Battery files are separate raw persistent RAM; use the expected exact size or export raw data from the originating emulator. Do not pad or truncate an unknown format.

details.title: Test failed or is inconclusive
details.text: Open Original, Build and Difference pictures where recorded. Check route, start state, frame, comparison region and assertion. An incomplete run is not a pass; a visual difference can be intended. Rerun after correcting the specific test setup or edit.

details.title: Draft save, backup or restore failed
details.text: Keep the window open and copy unsaved text. Check write access, available space and the active workspace. Do not remove an active writer's lock. Restore from a complete private backup or Trash, then recheck files and run fresh tests.

chapters.title: Use documented codes to find investigation leads
chapters.intro: A documented code can narrow a search. Its published effect label is a claim to test, and its CPU address still needs a valid mapping to the selected ROM.
steps: In Resources, expand ROM health & revision, then Code reference catalog. Choose a local UTF-8 TXT, JSON, JSONL, CSV or TSV catalog and click Import code references. This replaces the project’s reference catalog; it does not edit the ROM.
Choose Inspect matching references. Search an effect label or code and use Previous/Next for additional pages. Required + combinations and / revision alternatives remain distinct.

Read the revision status. MATCHED compares supplied hashes with the root source; MISMATCH has no mapped locations. UNSPECIFIED usually means title-only selection. Even a hash match does not verify the effect label.

Use Inspect beside a decoded location to open its bytes. Compare bytes can eliminate incompatible candidates, but a switchable-bank candidate does not establish the active bank. Do not turn an incomplete or truncated combination into a patch.
chapters.result: You can follow a source-attributed clue to actual bounded ROM bytes without silently activating a cheat or trusting another game’s offsets.
chapters.note: Game Genie decoding covers NES, SNES, Genesis, GB and GBC only. GBA codes use other formats and are not decoded here. Hardware overlays, unknown mappers and unsupported codes remain unresolved. Keep the original local catalog for full provenance when a result is shortened.

chapters.title: Inspect a shared engine without known game offsets
chapters.intro: The GBA recognizer follows a supported THUMB instruction pattern and validates linked player, song-header and track-pointer structures. It does not look up a Wario Land 4 address.
steps: Let deep scan finish, or choose Rescan ROM. Expand Recognized data structures in the ROM investigation panel when a finding is available.
Read the engine family, linked-record count and source reference. View Song table and the other location buttons open the actual file bytes used by this finding.

Separate a recognized structure from editing support. This recognizer checks one straight-line M4A-compatible loader and a bounded table ending at its first referenced header. Other drivers, compiler variants or table placements can be missed.

An ambiguous result selects no table. A work-budget result reports no complete finding. A no-match result does not prove that the engine is absent. Use a checked sample/sequence definition before editing music.
chapters.result: A supported shared format supplies useful locations even when a game-specific offset is unavailable.
chapters.note: Engine version, full sequence control flow, playback correctness, instruments and safe relocation are not certified. The current detector validates track bounds and a supported initial command, rather than interpreting every song. It does not create an editable commercial-game music definition.

chapters.title: Understand an address before investigating it
chapters.intro: A CPU address, file offset and video-memory offset can have the same number and refer to different things. Hardware help explains the region without pretending to know a game variable.
steps: Open More tools > Troubleshooting and expand Hardware & address help. A completed ROM scan supplies the CPU, byte-order convention, graphics layout and mapping notes for the selected system.
Choose the address domain, enter a decimal or 0x hexadecimal value, and click Explain address. NES PPU, physical VRAM and SNES audio CPU domains are separate choices only where supported.

Read the region and its conditions. A GB cartridge window may contain RTC registers; a SNES audio port is not audio RAM; Genesis sound RAM requires bus arbitration. Register descriptions never read or write the hardware.

For a persistent ROM edit, use Address explorer with a checked mapping, including the physical bank and header offset. A core’s exposed-memory offset also needs an established mapping before treating it as a CPU address.
chapters.result: You can tell a plausible ROM location from RAM, graphics storage, a device port or an unresolved board-dependent range.
chapters.note: To investigate a changing stat, reproduce one controlled change, narrow its RAM candidates, and establish the writer and immutable source in a debugger that exposes those events. ROMancer’s snapshots do not provide instruction breakpoints or prove causation. Unexecuted bytes and repeated FF/00 runs do not establish free space.

chapters.title: Read automatic cartridge verification
chapters.intro: Deep scan now displays individual cartridge-health results, including supported startup addresses. These checks describe the stored image without executing its program.
steps: Let the automatic scan finish. Expand Cartridge verification in ROM investigation. Read Consistent, Needs attention, Mismatch and Not checked separately. A warning is not a proof of corruption.

Inspect supported reset vectors or entry branches. CPU addresses and file locations remain different. Click a vector/header or target-byte button to examine its actual storage. An unresolved bank state does not receive a guessed target.

For GB/GBC/GBA, read the documented header checks. Logo comparison uses fingerprints rather than distributed logo assets; GBA normalization changes only documented variable bits. Custom headers can intentionally differ.

For ordinary LoROM/HiROM up to 4 MiB, checksum verification handles standard tail mirroring and an identified copier header. The size declaration uses the rounded-up payload size. Enhancement chips, extended maps and unresolved layouts remain outside this checksum rule.
chapters.result: A valid non-power-of-two standard SNES image can be checked correctly, and all six systems get startup checks within their supported mappings and encodings.
chapters.note: NES has no standard whole-cartridge checksum. A standard header logo and an in-bounds branch do not prove game identity, valid target instructions, authentic firmware, or successful gameplay. Use native capture for bounded actual access events. It is separate from these static cartridge checks and does not provide continuous live break/continue control.

details.text: The supported linear GBA cartridge format is limited to 32 MiB. An engine detector that reaches its own budget reports that limit separately; the other cartridge and resource checks remain available.

chapters.title: Investigate a changing value without a game profile
chapters.intro: ROMancer can gather evidence from an unfamiliar ROM. Start with one number or a controlled change rather than guessing a game property from byte values.
steps: Load and pause the selected ROM in Playtest, then open Investigation. Name the experiment and enter the visible number, or leave it blank for change-only tests.
Choose Capture before. Perform one controlled action, pause and capture again. Record whether the target increased, decreased, changed, or changed by an exact amount.
Add an unchanged control while unrelated activity continues. This helps reject background counters. Keep before, changed and control observations together.
Compare surviving RAM offsets, widths, byte order, signed/BCD encoding and display relationships. Additional observations help separate equally fitting hypotheses.
Use Add watch to retain a range or Investigate accesses for a native physical watch. Continue with the native capture chapter.
chapters.result: A source-bound observation history and tested numeric hypotheses, without a game-specific profile or a memory write.
chapters.note: Each observation covers at most 4096 bytes; an experiment keeps at most 32 observations. A new worker, reset or loaded state requires a fresh series. Restored project evidence remains historical and cannot supply fresh native proof.
